name: Google Cloud
tagline: Pay-as-you-go Compute Engine VMs for hosting sites and apps
description: Google Cloud's Compute Engine offers pay-as-you-go virtual machines for hosting websites and apps, with a permanently free e2-micro tier.
about: This entry covers Google Cloud narrowly as a website-hosting option — specifically Compute Engine virtual machines, with a brief mention of App Engine. Google Cloud Platform itself is a sprawling enterprise cloud with hundreds of services (BigQuery, Vertex AI, Kubernetes, networking, storage and more); none of that broader catalog is in scope here, only the slice comparable to a traditional web host.

Compute Engine bills by the second with no long-term contract. Entry-level shared-core machine types run: e2-micro (2 vCPU burstable to 1/8 core, 1 GB RAM) at roughly $0.0084/hour (~$6.11/month); e2-small (2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM) at roughly $0.0168/hour (~$12.23/month); and e2-medium (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM) at roughly $0.0335/hour (~$24.46/month) in the us-central1 region. These are on-demand list prices before any sustained-use or committed-use discounts, and Google Cloud's own pricing pages are the source of truth since regional and discount pricing shifts over time.

Google's Always Free tier includes one e2-micro instance per month in specific US regions (us-west1, us-central1, us-east1), plus 30 GB of standard persistent disk and 1 GB of network egress — enough to run a genuinely small site (a static page, a low-traffic blog, a personal project) at no cost indefinitely, as long as usage stays under those limits. Anything beyond that — more RAM, more traffic, a managed database, a CDN — starts accruing per-second charges, and there's no bundled domain, email or one-click WordPress installer the way a traditional shared host provides; you're provisioning and managing a bare Linux VM yourself (or via App Engine's more managed, but pricier, platform-as-a-service layer).
policies: Google Cloud runs on consumption-based billing rather than a subscription with a fixed refund window — you're charged for what you use, and unused free-trial credit (when offered to new accounts) simply expires rather than being refundable. There's no blanket money-back guarantee comparable to shared-hosting providers; check Google Cloud's own billing terms for the current new-account credit offer and any dispute process before committing real workloads.

Because pricing is metered per second across dozens of machine types, regions and discount programs (sustained-use, committed-use, spot VMs), the figures above are current list prices for entry-level shared-core instances only — always confirm against Google Cloud's live pricing page before budgeting, since GCP pricing changes more frequently than a typical hosting plan's fixed monthly rate.
